scenes.tts: In vertebrate skeletal muscle, a fibre shortens, yet none of its filaments gets shorter. How can that be? A fibre is one long cell, packed with chains of repeating units called sarcomeres. Each sarcomere holds thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin.
scenes.visual: a fibre bar shortens; red chips say no filament gets shorter and ask how; the bar divides into sarcomeres, one opens to thick myosin and thin actin bars
scenes.narration: In vertebrate skeletal muscle, a fibre shortens, yet none of its filaments gets shorter. How can that be? A fibre is one long cell, packed with chains of repeating units called sarcomeres. Each sarcomere holds thick filaments of myosin and thin filaments of actin.

scenes.tts: The signal starts at the neuromuscular junction, where a motor neuron meets the fibre. The neuron releases acetylcholine, which opens channels in the fibre's membrane. The membrane depolarizes, and an action potential travels along it. The signal runs down the T tubules, which are infoldings of the membrane reaching deep into the fibre.
scenes.visual: neuron ending above the fibre membrane; chemical dots cross the gap; signal dots run along the membrane and down three T tubule bars
scenes.narration: The signal starts at the neuromuscular junction, where a motor neuron meets the fibre. The neuron releases acetylcholine, which opens channels in the fibre's membrane. The membrane depolarizes, and an action potential travels along it. The signal runs down the T tubules, which are infoldings of the membrane reaching deep into the fibre.

scenes.tts: Next to each T tubule lies the sarcoplasmic reticulum. It is the fibre's internal calcium store. A voltage sensor in the T tubule membrane is linked to the store's calcium release channel. When the voltage changes, the sensor opens the channel, and calcium floods out. In vertebrate skeletal muscle, calcium entering from outside the cell is not required for this step.
scenes.visual: store boxes appear beside the tubules and fill with calcium; one pair enlarges; the sensor lights, the channel opens, calcium dots flood out

scenes.tts: Troponin is a complex of three proteins on the thin filament. Tropomyosin, a strand along the thin filament, covers the sites where myosin binds. Calcium binds troponin. Troponin then shifts tropomyosin, and the sites are uncovered. Myosin heads attach to actin, swing, and pull the thin filament toward the middle of the sarcomere. These attached heads are called cross-bridges.
scenes.visual: a thin filament with troponin and a covering strand; calcium binds, the strand slips aside, heads attach and swing, the filament moves

scenes.tts: This is the sliding filament model. The filaments do not get shorter. They slide past each other. The A band, the length of the thick filaments, keeps its width while the sarcomere shortens. Think of two combs pushed together, tooth into tooth. Each comb keeps its length. Only the overlap changes.
scenes.visual: the sarcomere shortens with thin bars sliding in; a bracket on the thick bars keeps its width; two combs slide together
scenes.narration: This is the sliding filament model. The filaments do not get shorter. They slide past each other. scenes.tts: In vertebrate skeletal muscle, A T P has two jobs. A T P binding to a myosin head releases it from actin. Splitting the A T P re-cocks the head for the next stroke. Separately, pumps in the store use A T P to move calcium back. As calcium falls, tropomyosin covers the sites again, and the muscle relaxes. Without A T P, the heads stay stuck to actin. That is why muscles stiffen after death. Keep this rule: filaments slide, and A T P lets the heads go.
scenes.visual: two panels: ATP releases and re-cocks a head; pumps return calcium and the strand covers the sites; then a stuck head with no ATP
